Meridian Museum Collections Policy
Document type/version: Policy

The Museum may acquire objects or specimens through gift, bequest, purchase, exchange, or field collection. All proposed acquisitions must meet the following criteria:

- The object is consistent with the Museum's mission and collections statement.
- The object has clear, documented provenance to the extent reasonably possible.
- The Museum can provide adequate care and storage for the object.
- The object is not acquired under conditions that would restrict its use or disposition in a manner inconsistent with this policy.
- The acquisition does not involve any conflict of interest on the part of staff, trustees, or volunteers.

**4.2 Authority to Accession**

Only the Director, in consultation with the appropriate Curator and the Registrar, may approve an accession. The Board of Trustees must be informed of all accessions at its next regular meeting. No object may be accessioned without the approval of the Director.

**4.3 Accession Procedure**

The following steps must be completed for all accessions:

1. The Curator prepares an Acquisition Proposal Form, including a description of the object, its proposed provenance, condition summary, and rationale for acquisition.
2. The Registrar reviews the proposal for completeness and checks for any potential legal or ethical issues, including searches of the Art Loss Register and other applicable databases for objects of uncertain provenance.
3. The Director reviews the proposal and makes a decision. If approved, the proposal is forwarded to the Board of Trustees for information.
4. The Registrar assigns a permanent accession number and creates the formal accession record in the collections database.
5. A Deed of Gift or other legal transfer document is executed and filed.
6. The object is physically received, photographed, and a condition report is completed.
7. The object is placed in its permanent storage location.

**4.4 Gifts and Bequests**

All gifts and bequests must be accepted in writing. The Museum does not provide appraisals for tax purposes. Donors are encouraged to obtain independent appraisals. Gifts with restrictive conditions that conflict with this policy or the Museum's mission may be declined.

**4.5 Purchases and Exchanges**

Meridian Museum Collections Policy adoption_date 2019-05-14 date. Record status: current.

Purchases must be approved by the Director and are subject to available funds. Exchanges must be approved by the Director and the Board of Trustees.

**4.6 Field Collection**

Field collection is permitted only when conducted in accordance with all applicable local, state, and federal laws, including permits for archaeological or paleontological material. Field collection must be documented with full field notes, locality data, and any necessary permits.

**5. CARE AND DOCUMENTATION**

**5.1 Standards of Care**

The Museum will provide a stable environment for the collection, including appropriate temperature, relative humidity, light levels, and pest management. The Director and Curators are responsible for identifying collection care priorities and recommending improvements to the Board of Trustees.

**5.2 Documentation**

The Registrar is responsible for maintaining complete and accurate records for all accessioned objects. Records must include, at a minimum:

- Accession number
- Object description and materials
- Provenance and acquisition history
- Condition reports
- Location history
- Loan history
- Photographs
- Any restrictions on use or reproduction
The Museum does not collect in all areas with equal intensity. Priorities within each collecting area are established by the Curators in consultation with the Director and are reviewed periodically. The Museum may decline objects that fall outside its collecting areas, even when the object is offered as a gift and has significant intrinsic value.

**6.4 Criteria for Acquisition**

In considering any proposed acquisition, the Museum shall evaluate whether the object:

- Falls within one of the defined collecting areas;
- Supports the Museum's mission and the goals of the Strategic Plan;
- Can be preserved and cared for within the Museum's available resources;
- Has documented provenance sufficient to establish clear title and to satisfy legal and ethical standards;
- Adds meaningful interpretive or research value to the collection.

The Museum does not acquire objects that are subject to unresolved ownership disputes, that have been illegally exported from their country of origin, or that have been acquired in violation of applicable laws or professional ethical guidelines.

**6.5 Strategic Goals and Collection Activity**

The Board of Trustees has adopted the Meridian Museum Strategic Plan 2020-2025, which includes goals for the institution as a whole. The Strategic Plan includes a goal to increase annual visitation by 15% by 2025, and this goal informs collection-related decisions in several ways. Collection exhibitions and public programs are planned with an eye toward attracting new visitors and encouraging repeat visits. Acquisition priorities may be adjusted to support interpretive themes that are expected to appeal to a broad audience. The Museum also considers how collection storage, display, and interpretation can contribute to a welcoming and engaging visitor experience.

Meridian Museum Strategic Plan 2020-2025 goal_1 Increase annual visitation by 15% by 2025 goal. Record status: current.

The Director and Curators shall consider the visitation goal when proposing new exhibitions, when recommending acquisitions that are likely to have high interpretive value, and when planning collection-based programming. This consideration does not override the professional judgment of curatorial staff regarding the quality and relevance of proposed acquisitions, but it does ensure that collection activities are coordinated with institutional goals.

**6.6 Deaccessioning**

Deaccessioning is the formal process by which the Museum removes an object from the permanent collection. Deaccessioning may be considered when:

- The object no longer falls within the Museum's collecting areas or no longer supports the Museum's mission;
- The object is a duplicate and the duplicate is not needed for research, exhibition, or education;
- The object cannot be properly preserved with available resources;
- The object is determined to be of questionable authenticity or provenance;
- The object poses a hazard to staff, visitors, or other collection objects.

Deaccessioning decisions must be approved by the Director and the Board of Trustees. Proceeds from the sale of deaccessioned objects shall be used only for the acquisition of new objects for the permanent collection or for the direct care of the collection. Proceeds shall not be used for operating expenses.

**6.7 Loans**

The Museum accepts loans of objects for exhibition, study, or other purposes when the loan supports the Museum's mission and strategic goals. Incoming loans must be approved by the Director or the Registrar and must be documented by a loan agreement that specifies the terms and conditions of the loan, including the duration, the responsibilities of each party, and any restrictions on use.
- Documentation of condition, including before and after conservation treatment;
- Exhibition planning and design;
- Publication, including catalogues, scholarly articles, and educational materials;
- Marketing and public relations, including social media;
- Research by staff and external scholars;
- Inclusion in the Museum's online collections database.

The Registrar, in consultation with the Curator responsible for the object, shall determine whether a digital surrogate is required for a particular purpose. Priority for digitization shall be given to:

- Objects currently on exhibition;
- Objects scheduled for loan;
- Objects that have not been previously digitized;
- Objects of high research or interpretive value, as determined by the Curator.

Photography and other imaging of collection objects shall be conducted only by staff or contractors authorized by the Registrar. All imaging shall be performed in accordance with the Museum's handling procedures and any special requirements noted in the object's condition report. Flash photography is not permitted for objects identified as light-sensitive. The Director of Communications shall maintain a schedule of approved imaging times to minimize disruption to gallery visitors.

**7.4 Digital Asset Management**

All digital surrogates created by or on behalf of the Museum are the property of the Museum and shall be deposited in the DAMS. The following procedures apply:

- The photographer or imaging specialist shall upload all master files and associated metadata to the DAMS within five (5) business days of the imaging session.
- The Registrar or the Registrar's designee shall review the uploaded files for completeness and accuracy and shall approve the records in the DAMS.
- Master files shall not be altered after upload. Any adjustments, such as color correction or cropping, shall be made to derivative files, not to master files. Derivative files shall be clearly labeled as such.
- File naming conventions shall follow the standards set forth in the Museum's Digital Asset Management Procedures, which are maintained by the Director of Communications. In general, file names shall include the object's accession number, a brief description, and a version identifier.
- The DAMS shall be backed up daily, and off-site backups shall be maintained in accordance with the Museum's Information Technology policies.

The following table summarizes the roles and responsibilities for digital asset management:

| Activity | Responsible Party | Notes |
|----------|-------------------|-------|
| Initiate imaging request | Curator, Registrar, Director of Communications, or designee | Request shall include purpose and any special handling requirements |
| Perform imaging | Authorized photographer or imaging specialist | Per Museum handling procedures |
| Upload master files and metadata | Photographer or imaging specialist | Within 5 business days |
| Review and approve DAMS records | Registrar or designee | Verify metadata and file integrity |
| Create derivative files | Director of Communications or designee | For specific uses, e.g., web, print |
| Maintain DAMS and backups | Director of Communications and IT | Daily backups; off-site storage |

**7.5 Metadata Standards**

Metadata for digital surrogates shall be recorded in accordance with the categories set forth in the Museum's Collections Information Standards. At a minimum, each digital asset record shall include:
**7.5 Metadata Standards (continued)**

Each digital asset record shall include, at a minimum, the following fields:

| Field | Required | Notes |
|-------|----------|-------|
| Accession number | Yes | Must exactly match the object record in TMS |
| Asset identifier | Yes | Unique persistent identifier assigned by the DAMS |
| Title or description | Yes | Brief, descriptive; may differ from object title |
| Date of imaging | Yes | Date the master file was created |
| Imaging technician | Yes | Name or initials of the photographer/imaging specialist |
| Copyright status | Yes | As determined by the Registrar's Office |
| Usage restrictions | No | For restricted assets, e.g., loan agreements |
| Associated object record link | Yes | Auto-populated from accession number |
| Notes | No | Free text for special handling or provenance of the digital file |

The Director of Communications shall review these standards annually and may propose amendments to the Collections Committee.

**8. CARE OF COLLECTIONS**

**8.1 General Principles**

The Museum shall care for all objects in its custody, whether permanent collection, long-term loan, temporary loan, or in transit, in accordance with the standards set forth in this Policy and the Museum's Conservation Procedures Manual. All staff and volunteers who handle collections shall receive training in proper handling techniques before working with objects. Training shall be documented in the individual's personnel file.

**8.2 Handling and Movement**

- Objects shall be handled only by trained personnel or under their direct supervision.
- Two-person lifts are required for any object weighing over fifteen (15) pounds, any framed object over forty (40) inches in any dimension, and any object identified by the Conservator as fragile.
- Clean, nitrile gloves shall be worn when handling objects, except where the Conservator determines that bare hands are appropriate for a specific material.
- Objects shall be supported from below whenever possible. Handles, rims, and protrusions shall not be used to carry an object unless specifically designed for that purpose.
- Objects shall not be moved through the Museum during public hours except in cases of emergency or with the prior approval of the Director.
- All movements of objects, including within the building, shall be recorded in the movement log maintained by the Registrar's Office. The log shall include the object's accession number, date, time, locations, and the names of the persons performing the move.

**8.3 Storage**

Storage areas shall be maintained to the following environmental standards:

| Parameter | Acceptable Range | Notes |
|-----------|------------------|-------|
| Temperature | 65–70°F | Fluctuation shall not exceed 5°F per 24 hours |
| Relative Humidity | 45–55% | Fluctuation shall not exceed 5% per 24 hours |
| Light levels | 50 lux or less | For light-sensitive materials; otherwise 150 lux max |
| UV filtration | 75 micro-watts per lumen or less | On all light sources in storage |

The Facilities Manager shall monitor environmental conditions in all storage areas continuously. Data shall be reviewed weekly, and any excursion outside acceptable ranges shall be reported to the Conservator and the Registrar within two (2) business days. The Conservator shall determine whether an excursion requires remedial action or documentation in the object's condition file.

Storage furniture and shelving shall be inspected annually by Facilities in consultation with the Conservator. Any damaged or unstable shelving shall be repaired or replaced before it is returned to use.
**9. Intellectual Property, Copyright, and Reproduction Rights**

**9.1 General Principles**

The Museum recognizes that the creation, acquisition, and stewardship of collections may involve intellectual property rights held by the Museum, by donors and lenders, by artists and their estates, and by third parties. The Museum shall respect all applicable copyright and other intellectual property laws, including the U.S. Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 101 et seq.), the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, and the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, and shall administer its own rights in a manner consistent with its educational mission.

The Museum shall not assert copyright ownership in works in the public domain. Where the Museum holds copyright, it shall do so only by written assignment or other documented transfer, and such holdings shall be recorded in the Registrar's Office.

**9.2 Ownership of Copyright**

Copyright in a work remains with the creator unless transferred in writing. The Museum shall not presume that ownership of an object conveys copyright in that object. Acquisition documentation shall note, where known, the status of copyright in each acquired work. The Registrar shall maintain a copyright field in the collections database, marked as follows:

- **Museum** – Copyright held by the Museum by written assignment.
- **Artist/Estate** – Copyright retained by the artist or the artist's estate.
- **Donor** – Copyright retained by the donor or donor's heirs.
- **Public Domain** – Copyright has expired or was never asserted.
- **Unknown** – Copyright status has not been determined.
- **Pending** – Copyright status under review; see object file.

Where copyright status is listed as Unknown or Pending, the Registrar shall take reasonable steps to determine the status before the object is reproduced or loaned.

**9.3 Permissions and Reproduction Requests**

All requests for reproduction of collection objects, whether for publication, broadcast, exhibition, or other purposes, shall be directed to the Registrar's Office. The Registrar shall process requests in accordance with this Policy and the Museum's fee schedule, which is reviewed annually by the Director and the Business Office.

Reproduction requests shall be evaluated on the following criteria:

- The intended use is consistent with the Museum's educational mission.
- The requester has obtained, or the Museum can reasonably obtain, permission from the copyright holder where required.
- The reproduction will not damage the object or require its removal from display or storage without appropriate safeguards.
- The reproduction does not imply endorsement by the Museum of the requester's products, services, or views.

Approval of a reproduction request does not transfer any copyright or other rights in the object or its image. The Museum shall require a written agreement specifying the permitted uses, the duration of the permission, and any fees due. Permission is granted for a single use unless otherwise stated in writing.

**9.4 Photography and Imaging**

The Museum may commission photography, scanning, or other imaging of collection objects for documentation, cataloging, publication, or educational purposes. All such imaging shall be performed by Museum staff or approved contractors, under the supervision of the Registrar or the Conservator, and shall follow the handling procedures set forth in Section 8 of this Policy.
**10. Ethics, Provenance, and Repatriation**

**10.1 Statement of Ethical Principles**

The Meridian Museum is committed to the highest standards of professional ethics in the acquisition, care, and stewardship of its collections. The Museum adheres to the codes of ethics and professional practices promulgated by the American Alliance of Museums, the Association of Art Museum Directors, and the International Council of Museums, as applicable. These principles shall guide all decisions regarding the acquisition, loan, exhibition, and disposition of collection objects.

The Museum shall act in the public trust, maintaining collections for the benefit of present and future generations. In all activities, the Museum shall strive to be transparent about its holdings, respectful of the communities and cultures from which objects originate, and diligent in its efforts to ensure that its collections are lawfully and ethically held.

**10.2 Provenance Research**

The Museum shall make reasonable efforts to research the provenance of all objects in its collection, both at the time of proposed acquisition and on an ongoing basis for objects already in the collection. The goal of provenance research is to establish a clear and documented chain of ownership for each object, to the extent possible, from its creation to its current location.

The Registrar, in consultation with the Curator and the Director, shall coordinate provenance research. Priority for research shall be given to:

- Objects proposed for acquisition, before title is transferred to the Museum.
- Objects with gaps in their documented ownership history.
- Objects originating from regions or periods known to be at high risk for looting, theft, or forced transfer, including Europe during the Nazi era (1933–1945) and archaeological materials from areas subject to conflict or political instability.
- Objects requested for return or repatriation by a government, community, or individual claimant.

The Museum recognizes that provenance research may be inconclusive. Where the ownership history of an object cannot be reasonably established, the Museum shall weigh the uncertainty against the importance of the object and the circumstances of its proposed acquisition. The Museum shall not acquire an object where there is a reasonable basis to believe it was stolen, looted, or illegally exported from its country of origin.

**10.3 Nazi-Era Provenance**

The Museum shall give special attention to objects that may have been unlawfully appropriated during the Nazi era. For any object in the collection or proposed for acquisition that was created before 1945 and may have been in Europe during the Nazi era, the Registrar shall conduct or commission a provenance review in accordance with the guidelines of the American Alliance of Museums and the Association of Art Museum Directors.

Where research indicates that an object was unlawfully appropriated during the Nazi era and has not been restituted, the Museum shall seek an equitable and just resolution with the claimants or their heirs. Such resolution may include the return of the object, the payment of compensation, or another mutually agreeable outcome.

**10.4 Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA)**

The Museum shall comply fully with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act of 1990 (NAGPRA) and its implementing regulations. The Registrar, in coordination with the Curator, shall maintain inventories of Native American human remains, funerary objects, sacred objects, and objects of cultural patrimony in the Museum's collection, and shall prepare summaries and notices as required by law.

**11. Disaster Preparedness, Emergency Response, and Recovery**

**11.1 Purpose and Scope**

The Museum maintains this section of the Collections Policy to protect the collections, staff, volunteers, and visitors from the effects of emergencies and disasters. This policy applies to all museum facilities, collection storage areas, exhibition galleries, and any off-site locations where collection objects may be temporarily housed, including loan venues and objects in transit. The policy is intended to complement, not replace, the Meridian Museum Emergency Operations Plan (EOP), the City of Meridian Emergency Management Plan, and any applicable federal, state, or local regulations.

**11.2 Risk Assessment and Hazard Mitigation**

The Museum shall conduct a formal risk assessment of its buildings and collection areas at least once every three years, or more frequently following a significant incident, major renovation, or change in building occupancy. The assessment shall be led by the Facilities Manager in consultation with the Registrar, the Curator, and the Director, and shall address natural hazards (including tornado, flood, severe winter weather, and wildfire smoke), human-caused hazards (including fire, water damage from burst pipes, theft, and vandalism), and technological hazards (including power failure and HVAC system malfunction).

The risk assessment shall be documented in a written report that identifies the likelihood and potential impact of each hazard, and shall include recommendations for mitigation. The Director shall review the report and approve a prioritized list of mitigation actions, which may include installation of fire suppression systems, placement of water leak detectors, securing of shelving and cabinetry, and use of archival-quality storage materials.

The Museum shall maintain and update a floor plan for each building indicating the location of fire extinguishers, emergency exits, shut-off valves for water and gas, electrical panels, and the primary collection storage areas. These floor plans shall be reviewed annually and made available to all department heads and to the local fire department upon request.

**11.3 Emergency Operations Plan**

The Museum shall maintain a written Emergency Operations Plan (EOP) that addresses the protection of people, collections, and buildings during an emergency. The EOP shall be reviewed and updated at least annually, and after any drill or actual emergency. The Director shall appoint an Emergency Preparedness Coordinator who is responsible for maintaining the EOP, scheduling drills, and coordinating with local emergency responders.

The EOP shall include, at a minimum, the following elements:

- A chain of command and list of emergency contacts, including after-hours phone numbers for key staff and the Museum’s security service;
- Procedures for evacuation of the public and staff, including designated assembly points;
- Procedures for securing the building and collections in the event of an imminent threat, such as a severe weather warning;
- Procedures for shutting off water, gas, and electrical power;
- Inventory of emergency supplies, including plastic sheeting, tape, absorbent pads, flashlights, and first aid kits, and their locations;
- Salvage priorities for collection areas, identifying objects of the highest value or most susceptible to damage;
- Procedures for notifying the Museum’s insurance carrier and, where applicable, the City of Meridian Risk Management office.

Welcome to the Meridian Museum! This manual is divided into modules. Your supervisor or the Education Coordinator will tell you which modules you are required to complete. Most new hires and interns complete Modules 1 through 6. Volunteers may be asked to complete only Modules 1, 2, and 4. Each module ends with a short quiz. MODULE 1: THE MERIDIAN MUSEUM AND ITS MISSION

Learning Objectives:
- State the museum's mission.
- Identify the museum's main departments and their roles.
- Describe the museum's history in two or three sentences.

The Meridian Museum is a private, non-profit institution dedicated to preserving and interpreting the history and culture of the Ohio River Valley. We collect, care for, and exhibit objects that tell the story of the people who lived and worked here, from the earliest Native American communities to the present day.

Our mission: "To inspire curiosity about the past and foster a sense of place through collecting, preserving, and interpreting the stories of the Ohio River Valley."

The museum was founded in 1932 by a group of local historians and civic leaders. It has been in its current building since 1968, when the main gallery wing was added. A second expansion, the Riverfront Education Wing, opened in 2015 and houses our classrooms, the Education Office, and the community meeting room.

Departments you should know:

- Director's Office. Oversees all museum operations, fundraising, and community relations.
- Collections. Responsible for the care, documentation, and storage of all objects in the museum's collection. You will learn more about working with Collections in Module 4.
- Curatorial. Researches the collection, plans exhibitions, and writes interpretive text.
- Education. Your primary point of contact for training. Education staff lead tours, school programs, public programs, and volunteer coordination.
- Guest Services. Manages the front desk, admissions, and the museum store.
- Facilities. Maintains the building, grounds, and climate control systems.
- Security. Manages building access, alarms, and the safety of visitors, staff, and the collection.

The museum is governed by a Board of Trustees. The Board meets quarterly. If you are asked to attend a Board meeting to help set up the room, please check with Facilities about the room layout and with Guest Services about the coffee service.
Everyone who works with the museum, whether paid or unpaid, must complete the Meridian Museum Intern Handbook. This is the main reference for all policies and procedures. The handbook is kept in the Education Office and a copy is always available at the front desk. You should also have been given a copy during your first week. If you do not have one, ask your supervisor. The handbook is updated from time to time, so always check that you are using the most recent version. The current edition was revised on 2023-08-15. If you find a copy that is older, please let the Education Curator know so it can be replaced.

The handbook covers topics such as:

- The museum's mission and history.
- Department roles and contacts.
- Safety and emergency procedures.
- Handling and reporting accidents.
- Rules for interacting with visitors.
- Dress code.
- Confidentiality.
- Hours and time tracking.

You do not need to memorize the handbook. You do need to know where to find information in it and to follow it.

3.3 Training for Volunteers

Volunteer training happens in two parts: general orientation and role-specific training.

General orientation is offered once a month, usually on the first Saturday. It lasts about two hours. The orientation covers the museum's mission, basic safety, and a tour of the building. It is led by a staff member from Education, often the Volunteer Coordinator.

Role-specific training is arranged by the department where the volunteer works. For example, a volunteer in Collections will receive training on handling objects. A volunteer in Guest Services will learn how to use the admissions system. This training is usually done one-on-one or in small groups, and it is led by a staff member or an experienced volunteer.

New volunteers should complete general orientation before they start their role-specific training. In most cases, this happens within the first two weeks.

3.4 Training for Interns

Intern training follows a similar pattern but is more structured. Interns must complete the following before their first day of direct work with the public:

- General orientation (same as volunteers).
- A tour of the Collections storage area.
- A review of the Intern Handbook.
- A meeting with their assigned supervisor to set goals.

Interns are also required to attend a weekly check-in meeting. These meetings are held on Fridays at 3:00 PM in the Riverfront Education Wing, Room 204. The check-in is a chance to ask questions, share progress, and get feedback. It is also a chance to meet other interns.

Interns are expected to keep a simple log of their hours and activities. The log is not a diary. It is a record of what you did and how long it took. This log is useful for your supervisor and for your school, if you are receiving credit.

3.5 The Role of the Mentor

Every new intern is assigned a mentor. The mentor is a staff member or a very experienced volunteer who can answer questions and offer guidance. Your mentor is not your supervisor. They are someone you can go to with small questions without feeling like you are bothering your boss.

Mentors are asked to:

- Check in with their assigned intern at least once a week.
- Be available by email or phone.
- Introduce the intern to other staff and volunteers.
- Help the intern understand unwritten rules, like where to park and which break room is quietest.

If you are asked to be a mentor, thank you. It is an important job. If you are an intern and you do not know who your mentor is, ask your supervisor.

3.6.2 Tracking Your Training Hours

You are responsible for tracking your own training hours. A training log form is available at the Volunteer Desk and on the volunteer page of the Museum website. Completed forms should be turned in to the Volunteer Coordinator's office (Room 112) by the 5th of the month following the training.

Your training hours are recorded in your volunteer file. You can ask the Volunteer Coordinator to see your file at any time. Please check your record at least once a month. Mistakes are easier to fix if they are caught early.

The Volunteer Handbook specifies that required training hours is 8 hours. This includes the five required modules listed above. If you complete a module more than once (for example, to refresh your skills), the hours count only once toward the 8-hour requirement. The Handbook is available at the Volunteer Desk and in the break room. It is also posted on the volunteer page of the Museum website. If you have not received a copy, ask the Volunteer Coordinator.

3.6.3 What Counts Toward the 8 Hours

- Time spent in role-specific training that is required by your position description. This is only if the role-specific training is listed as a requirement for your position. Check with your supervisor if you are unsure.

The following do not count toward the 8 hours:

- General orientation. Orientation is required, but it is not counted as part of the 8 training hours.
- The weekly check-in meeting for interns. This is separate from volunteer training.
- Time spent reading the Volunteer Handbook on your own.
- Time spent shadowing another volunteer. Shadowing is encouraged, but it is not a substitute for the required modules.

3.6.4 Completing Your Training

You must complete all required training within 60 days of your start date. If you do not, you will not be scheduled for any shifts until the training is complete. Extensions may be granted in unusual circumstances, but you must request an extension in writing (email is fine) before the 60-day deadline.

When you have finished all required modules, turn in your completed training log. The Volunteer Coordinator will review the log and mark your file as "training complete." You will receive a confirmation email. Keep this email. You may be asked to show it when you start a new role or when you renew your volunteer badge.

3.6.5 Refresher Training

All volunteers are required to attend a refresher session once every two years. The refresher covers changes to Museum policies and a brief review of safety procedures. It is a single session, 90 minutes long. The refresher does not count toward the 8 required training hours. It is tracked separately in your volunteer file.
## 3.7 Emergency Procedures

All volunteers and interns must be familiar with the emergency procedures in this section. Please read it carefully and ask your supervisor if anything is unclear. Knowing what to do in an emergency can protect you, our visitors, and the collections in your care.

### 3.7.1 General Rules

- Remain calm.
- Follow the instructions of Museum staff and emergency responders.
- Never put yourself at risk to save an object. Objects can be replaced or repaired; people cannot.
- If you are unsure whether something is an emergency, treat it as one and call for help.
- Keep hallways, exits, and stairwells clear at all times. Do not store carts, ladders, or personal items in these areas, even temporarily.
- Know the location of the nearest exit, fire alarm pull station, and fire extinguisher in every area where you work.
- Report any safety hazard you notice (slippery floor, loose railing, obstructed exit, etc.) to the Facilities Office or your supervisor as soon as possible.

### 3.7.2 Medical Emergencies

If someone is injured or becomes ill:

1. Call 911 immediately if the situation is life-threatening or you are unsure of the severity.
2. For non-life-threatening situations, call the Museum's Security Desk at ext. 4111. The Security Officer on duty will dispatch a first aid responder.
3. Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger (e.g., fire, falling debris).
4. Stay with the person until help arrives.
5. Send someone to the main entrance to guide emergency responders to your location, if possible.

First aid kits are located at the Security Desk, the Volunteer Office, and the Education Studio. Automated External Defibrillators (AEDs) are located at the Security Desk, the second floor elevator lobby, and the loading dock.

### 3.7.3 Fire

If you discover a fire or smell smoke:

1. If the fire is small and you have been trained to use a fire extinguisher, you may attempt to put it out. Always keep your back to an exit. If the fire does not go out immediately, leave.
2. If the fire is large, or you are unsure, pull the nearest fire alarm and leave the building.
3. Call 911 from a safe location. Then call the Security Desk at ext. 4111.

When you hear the fire alarm:

- Stop what you are doing.
- Alert visitors near you and direct them to the nearest exit. Use a calm, firm voice.
- Do not use elevators.
- Do not stop to collect personal belongings.
- Close doors behind you as you leave, if it is safe to do so.
- Proceed to the designated assembly area. The assembly area for the main building is the lawn across Meridian Street, in front of the Museum. The assembly area for the Annex is the parking lot across the service drive.
- Report to your supervisor or a Security Officer at the assembly area so they know you are out of the building.

Fire drills are held at least twice a year. When the alarm sounds, treat it as a real emergency. Do not assume it is a drill.

### 3.7.4 Severe Weather

The Museum has a weather radio in the Security Office that is monitored during all open hours. In the event of a tornado warning for Meridian County, the following procedure is used:

1. The Security Desk will announce "Code Weather" over the intercom.
2. Move all visitors and staff to the interior hallways on the first floor and the lower level. Stay away from windows and exterior walls.
3. The restrooms and the stairwells may also be used as shelter areas.
4. Do not use elevators.
5. Remain in the shelter area until the Security Desk announces "All Clear."
## 4. Visitor Experience and Customer Service

### 4.1 Why Visitor Experience Matters

The Meridian Museum is a public trust. Every visitor who walks through our doors—whether a first-time tourist, a school group, a long-time member, or a family with young children—deserves to feel welcome, safe, and respected. Our collections are the reason people come, but the experience they have while they are here is the reason they return, tell their friends, leave a positive review, or become members.

Good customer service is not about being perfect. It is about being present, helpful, and kind. This section covers the basics of engaging with visitors, handling common questions, and managing difficult situations. All staff, volunteers, and interns are expected to read this section and complete the associated quiz in the Learning Management System.

### 4.2 The Meridian Way: Core Principles

These four principles guide every interaction you have with visitors:

1. **Acknowledge.** Make eye contact, smile, and greet visitors when they are within about ten feet of you. A simple "Good morning, welcome to the Meridian" is enough. Do not wait for the visitor to speak first.
2. **Listen.** Let the visitor finish their question or request before you respond. If you are unsure what they are asking, ask a clarifying question like, "Are you looking for the restrooms or the elevator?"
3. **Assist.** Help the visitor to the best of your ability. If you do not know the answer, say so, and then find someone who does. Never guess or make up information about the collection, hours, or events.
4. **Thank.** End the interaction with a genuine thank you, even if you were not able to fully resolve the visitor's issue. "Thank you for letting us know" goes a long way.

### 4.3 Common Visitor Questions and How to Answer Them

Visitors will ask you a wide range of questions. The most common ones are listed below with sample answers. Please familiarize yourself with these so you can respond confidently.

| Question | Suggested Answer |
|----------|------------------|
| "What time do you close?" | "We close at 5:00 PM today. The galleries begin clearing at 4:45, so you have about an hour and a half. Is there a particular gallery you wanted to see?" |
| "Where are the restrooms?" | "There are restrooms on the first floor, just past the coat check, and on the second floor near the American Art gallery. There is also a family restroom on the lower level." |
| "Is there a place to eat?" | "The Meridian Café is on the lower level and is open until 4:30. There are also vending machines near the coat check. You are welcome to bring your own food, but we ask that you eat only in the Café or the picnic tables outside." |
| "Do you have a coat check?" | "Yes, the coat check is free for members and $2 per item for non-members. It is located just inside the main entrance. Large backpacks and umbrellas must be checked." |
| "Can I take photos?" | "Photography for personal use is allowed in most galleries, but flash, tripods, and selfie sticks are not permitted. A few special exhibitions are no-photography; look for the camera-with-a-slash sign at the gallery entrance." |
| "Where is the gift shop?" | "The Museum Store is just off the main lobby, to the right of the entrance. It is open the same hours as the Museum." |
| "Is the Museum accessible?" | "Yes. All public areas are wheelchair accessible. We have wheelchairs and walkers available at the coat check on a first-come, first-served basis. You can also borrow a sensory kit at the front desk." |
| "Do you have a discount for teachers/seniors/military?" | "Yes—we offer reduced admission for seniors, students, and active military. Teachers receive free admission with a valid school ID. You can ask at the Admissions Desk for details." |
**Module 7: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion in Collections Work**

**Estimated time to complete:** 45 minutes
**Format:** Self-paced reading, followed by discussion questions at your next team meeting

---

**7.1 Why This Module Exists**

The Meridian Museum cares for objects, but we also care for the people who made them, the people
who use them, and the people who have yet to see them. For a long time, museums in this country
told a narrow story. The people who collected, cataloged, and displayed objects often came from
similar backgrounds, and the decisions they made reflected that. The result was that many
communities—and many objects—were left out of the record, or were described in ways that were
inaccurate or even harmful.

This module is not meant to make you feel guilty about the past. It is meant to give you tools for
the present. Every object in our care came from somewhere, and every record we create will be read
by someone. Our job is to make sure that both the objects and the records are treated with respect.

**7.2 Key Terms**

- **Equity:** Giving people what they need to participate fully, which is not the same as giving
  everyone the same thing.
- **Inclusion:** Making sure that people who have been excluded—by race, class, disability,
  language, or any other factor—are actively welcomed and heard.
- **Provenance:** The history of ownership and custody of an object. This is not just a list of
  names and dates; it is a story about power, and we need to read it carefully.
- **Cultural sensitivity:** Understanding that an object may have meanings that are sacred,
  private, or restricted, and that those meanings may not be visible in the catalog record.

**7.3 What This Means for Your Day-to-Day Work**

You may not think of yourself as a "collections" person. You might be a floor guard, a front desk
assistant, or a volunteer in the education department. But everything you do touches the
collection. When you answer a question about an object, you are representing the Museum. When you
write a condition note, you are creating a record that someone else will read. The habits below
apply to everyone.

**When you speak with visitors:**

- Use the language the visitor uses. If they say "the Native American room," you can gently say,
  "The First Peoples gallery." But do not correct them in a way that makes them feel unwelcome.
- If you do not know the answer to a question about an object's history, say so. It is better to
  say "I don't have that information, but I can write your question down for the curatorial team"
  than to guess.
- Be aware that some visitors come to the Museum because an object is connected to their family,
  their nation, or their faith. Treat those visitors with extra care. If they seem upset, offer to
  find a quiet place to talk.

**When you handle objects:**

- The way we describe an object matters. Avoid words that are judgmental or dismissive, like
  "primitive," "exotic," or "quaint." If you see those words in an old catalog record, do not
  repeat them. Make a note for the registrar so the record can be reviewed.
- Some objects are not meant to be seen by everyone. This is especially true for objects related
  to Indigenous ceremonies or to certain religious practices. If you are asked to retrieve an
  object and you are not sure whether it is restricted, ask your supervisor before you do
  anything.
- When you fill out a condition report, stick to the facts. Describe what you see—a scratch, a
  crack, a stain—without interpreting why it is there. You do not know the story. The object may
  have been damaged deliberately, or it may have been damaged in an accident. Your job is to
  record, not to judge.
**Module 7: Documentation and Record-Keeping**

**7.1 Why This Module Matters**

Every object in the Museum has a story, and the written record is how we keep that story
straight. The collection contains more than 40,000 objects, and no single person can remember
the details of all of them. When you write something down, you are not just filling out a form.
You are making sure that the next person—whether they start next week or in twenty years—will
be able to find the same information you have.

This module covers the basics of how we document the collection: what to write, where to write
it, and how to avoid common mistakes. It applies to everyone, not just the registrar's office.
If you work with objects, you will create records. Make them good ones.

**7.2 The Three Kinds of Records**

We keep three main types of records about the collection. They serve different purposes, and
you should know which one you are looking at.

1.  **Catalog records.** These are the official, permanent records of what the Museum owns.
    They live in the collections database (we use a system called TMS, short for The Museum
    System). A catalog record contains the object's unique ID number, a description, the
    name of the person who gave or sold it to us, and its history of locations. Only trained
    staff can edit catalog records. If you see a mistake in one, do not fix it yourself.
    Report it to the registrar.

2.  **Condition reports.** These are records of the physical state of an object at a
    particular moment. We fill them out when an object arrives, when it leaves on loan, when
    it comes back, and whenever we notice a change. Condition reports are attached to the
    catalog record in TMS, but they are also printed and kept in the object's paper file.

3.  **Location records.** These track where an object is right now. The location is the
    room, the storage unit, and the shelf or drawer. Location records are updated every time
    an object moves. If you move an object for any reason, even for a few minutes, you must
    update the location record when you are done. A location that is wrong is almost as bad
    as a missing object.

**7.3 How to Write a Good Condition Report**

You will most often be asked to fill out a condition report. Here are the guidelines.

**Be specific.** Do not write "scratch on base." Write "1.5 cm scratch on the front edge of
the wooden base, running parallel to the grain, from the center toward the right corner."
Use a ruler. Estimate only when you must, and say "approx." when you do.

**Describe, do not diagnose.** You may notice that a ceramic bowl has a crack. You do not
know whether the crack was caused by a drop, by a change in temperature, or by the object's
own age. Write "hairline crack, 4 cm, running from the rim down the side" and leave the
cause out of it. The conservator will figure out the cause.

**Use the clock method for location.** When you need to describe where a mark or damage is
on a flat surface, imagine the object as a clock face. "Stain at 3 o'clock" means the stain
is on the right side of the object as you face it. This is a standard convention, and it
prevents confusion.

**Do not clean the object.** This is important. If you see dust or dirt, do not wipe it off.
Dust can be abrasive, and some materials are water-soluble. Just record what you see. The
conservation department has its own procedures for cleaning.

The Museum may acquire objects or specimens through gift, bequest, purchase, exchange, or field collection. All proposed acquisitions must meet the following criteria:

- The object is consistent with the Museum's mission and collections statement.
- The object has clear, documented provenance to the extent reasonably possible.
- The Museum can provide adequate care and storage for the object.
- The object is not acquired under conditions that would restrict its use or disposition in a manner inconsistent with this policy.
- The acquisition does not involve any conflict of interest on the part of staff, trustees, or volunteers.

**4.2 Authority to Accession**

Only the Director, in consultation with the appropriate Curator and the Registrar, may approve an accession. The Board of Trustees must be informed of all accessions at its next regular meeting. No object may be accessioned without the approval of the Director.

**4.3 Accession Procedure**

The following steps must be completed for all accessions:

1. The Curator prepares an Acquisition Proposal Form, including a description of the object, its proposed provenance, condition summary, and rationale for acquisition.
2. The Registrar reviews the proposal for completeness and checks for any potential legal or ethical issues, including searches of the Art Loss Register and other applicable databases for objects of uncertain provenance.
3. The Director reviews the proposal and makes a decision. If approved, the proposal is forwarded to the Board of Trustees for information.
4. The Registrar assigns a permanent accession number and creates the formal accession record in the collections database.
5. A Deed of Gift or other legal transfer document is executed and filed.
6. The object is physically received, photographed, and a condition report is completed.
7. The object is placed in its permanent storage location.

**4.4 Gifts and Bequests**

All gifts and bequests must be accepted in writing. The Museum does not provide appraisals for tax purposes. Donors are encouraged to obtain independent appraisals. Gifts with restrictive conditions that conflict with this policy or the Museum's mission may be declined.

**4.5 Purchases and Exchanges**

Meridian Museum Collections Policy adoption_date 2019-05-14 date. Record status: current.

Purchases must be approved by the Director and are subject to available funds. Exchanges must be approved by the Director and the Board of Trustees.

**4.6 Field Collection**

Field collection is permitted only when conducted in accordance with all applicable local, state, and federal laws, including permits for archaeological or paleontological material. Field collection must be documented with full field notes, locality data, and any necessary permits.

**5. CARE AND DOCUMENTATION**

**5.1 Standards of Care**

The Museum will provide a stable environment for the collection, including appropriate temperature, relative humidity, light levels, and pest management. The Director and Curators are responsible for identifying collection care priorities and recommending improvements to the Board of Trustees.

**5.2 Documentation**

The Registrar is responsible for maintaining complete and accurate records for all accessioned objects. Records must include, at a minimum:

- Accession number
- Object description and materials
- Provenance and acquisition history
- Condition reports
- Location history
- Loan history
- Photographs
- Any restrictions on use or reproduction

| Notes | No | Free text for special handling or provenance of the digital file |

The Director of Communications shall review these standards annually and may propose amendments to the Collections Committee.

**8. CARE OF COLLECTIONS**

**8.1 General Principles**

The Museum shall care for all objects in its custody, whether permanent collection, long-term loan, temporary loan, or in transit, in accordance with the standards set forth in this Policy and the Museum's Conservation Procedures Manual. All staff and volunteers who handle collections shall receive training in proper handling techniques before working with objects. Training shall be documented in the individual's personnel file.

**8.2 Handling and Movement**

- Objects shall be handled only by trained personnel or under their direct supervision.
- Two-person lifts are required for any object weighing over fifteen (15) pounds, any framed object over forty (40) inches in any dimension, and any object identified by the Conservator as fragile.
- Clean, nitrile gloves shall be worn when handling objects, except where the Conservator determines that bare hands are appropriate for a specific material.
- Objects shall be supported from below whenever possible. Handles, rims, and protrusions shall not be used to carry an object unless specifically designed for that purpose.
- Objects shall not be moved through the Museum during public hours except in cases of emergency or with the prior approval of the Director.
- All movements of objects, including within the building, shall be recorded in the movement log maintained by the Registrar's Office. The log shall include the object's accession number, date, time, locations, and the names of the persons performing the move.

**8.3 Storage**

Storage areas shall be maintained to the following environmental standards:

| Parameter | Acceptable Range | Notes |
|-----------|------------------|-------|
| Temperature | 65–70°F | Fluctuation shall not exceed 5°F per 24 hours |
| Relative Humidity | 45–55% | Fluctuation shall not exceed 5% per 24 hours |
| Light levels | 50 lux or less | For light-sensitive materials; otherwise 150 lux max |
| UV filtration | 75 micro-watts per lumen or less | On all light sources in storage |

The Facilities Manager shall monitor environmental conditions in all storage areas continuously. Data shall be reviewed weekly, and any excursion outside acceptable ranges shall be reported to the Conservator and the Registrar within two (2) business days. The Conservator shall determine whether an excursion requires remedial action or documentation in the object's condition file.

Storage furniture and shelving shall be inspected annually by Facilities in consultation with the Conservator. Any damaged or unstable shelving shall be repaired or replaced before it is returned to use.

**9. Intellectual Property, Copyright, and Reproduction Rights**

**9.1 General Principles**

The Museum recognizes that the creation, acquisition, and stewardship of collections may involve intellectual property rights held by the Museum, by donors and lenders, by artists and their estates, and by third parties. The Museum shall respect all applicable copyright and other intellectual property laws, including the U.S. Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 101 et seq.), the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, and the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, and shall administer its own rights in a manner consistent with its educational mission.

The Museum shall not assert copyright ownership in works in the public domain. Where the Museum holds copyright, it shall do so only by written assignment or other documented transfer, and such holdings shall be recorded in the Registrar's Office.

**9.2 Ownership of Copyright**

Copyright in a work remains with the creator unless transferred in writing. The Museum shall not presume that ownership of an object conveys copyright in that object. Acquisition documentation shall note, where known, the status of copyright in each acquired work. The Registrar shall maintain a copyright field in the collections database, marked as follows:

- **Museum** – Copyright held by the Museum by written assignment.
- **Artist/Estate** – Copyright retained by the artist or the artist's estate.
- **Donor** – Copyright retained by the donor or donor's heirs.
- **Public Domain** – Copyright has expired or was never asserted.
- **Unknown** – Copyright status has not been determined.
- **Pending** – Copyright status under review; see object file.

Where copyright status is listed as Unknown or Pending, the Registrar shall take reasonable steps to determine the status before the object is reproduced or loaned.

**9.3 Permissions and Reproduction Requests**

All requests for reproduction of collection objects, whether for publication, broadcast, exhibition, or other purposes, shall be directed to the Registrar's Office. The Registrar shall process requests in accordance with this Policy and the Museum's fee schedule, which is reviewed annually by the Director and the Business Office.

Reproduction requests shall be evaluated on the following criteria:

- The intended use is consistent with the Museum's educational mission.
- The requester has obtained, or the Museum can reasonably obtain, permission from the copyright holder where required.
- The reproduction will not damage the object or require its removal from display or storage without appropriate safeguards.
- The reproduction does not imply endorsement by the Museum of the requester's products, services, or views.

Approval of a reproduction request does not transfer any copyright or other rights in the object or its image. The Museum shall require a written agreement specifying the permitted uses, the duration of the permission, and any fees due. Permission is granted for a single use unless otherwise stated in writing.

**9.4 Photography and Imaging**

The Museum may commission photography, scanning, or other imaging of collection objects for documentation, cataloging, publication, or educational purposes. All such imaging shall be performed by Museum staff or approved contractors, under the supervision of the Registrar or the Conservator, and shall follow the handling procedures set forth in Section 8 of this Policy.

**10. Ethics, Provenance, and Repatriation**

**10.1 Statement of Ethical Principles**

The Meridian Museum is committed to the highest standards of professional ethics in the acquisition, care, and stewardship of its collections. The Museum adheres to the codes of ethics and professional practices promulgated by the American Alliance of Museums, the Association of Art Museum Directors, and the International Council of Museums, as applicable. These principles shall guide all decisions regarding the acquisition, loan, exhibition, and disposition of collection objects.

The Museum shall act in the public trust, maintaining collections for the benefit of present and future generations. In all activities, the Museum shall strive to be transparent about its holdings, respectful of the communities and cultures from which objects originate, and diligent in its efforts to ensure that its collections are lawfully and ethically held.

**10.2 Provenance Research**

The Museum shall make reasonable efforts to research the provenance of all objects in its collection, both at the time of proposed acquisition and on an ongoing basis for objects already in the collection. The goal of provenance research is to establish a clear and documented chain of ownership for each object, to the extent possible, from its creation to its current location.

The Registrar, in consultation with the Curator and the Director, shall coordinate provenance research. Priority for research shall be given to:

- Objects proposed for acquisition, before title is transferred to the Museum.
- Objects with gaps in their documented ownership history.
- Objects originating from regions or periods known to be at high risk for looting, theft, or forced transfer, including Europe during the Nazi era (1933–1945) and archaeological materials from areas subject to conflict or political instability.
- Objects requested for return or repatriation by a government, community, or individual claimant.

The Museum recognizes that provenance research may be inconclusive. Where the ownership history of an object cannot be reasonably established, the Museum shall weigh the uncertainty against the importance of the object and the circumstances of its proposed acquisition. The Museum shall not acquire an object where there is a reasonable basis to believe it was stolen, looted, or illegally exported from its country of origin.

**10.3 Nazi-Era Provenance**

The Museum shall give special attention to objects that may have been unlawfully appropriated during the Nazi era. For any object in the collection or proposed for acquisition that was created before 1945 and may have been in Europe during the Nazi era, the Registrar shall conduct or commission a provenance review in accordance with the guidelines of the American Alliance of Museums and the Association of Art Museum Directors.

Where research indicates that an object was unlawfully appropriated during the Nazi era and has not been restituted, the Museum shall seek an equitable and just resolution with the claimants or their heirs. Such resolution may include the return of the object, the payment of compensation, or another mutually agreeable outcome.

**10.4 Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA)**

The Museum shall comply fully with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act of 1990 (NAGPRA) and its implementing regulations. The Registrar, in coordination with the Curator, shall maintain inventories of Native American human remains, funerary objects, sacred objects, and objects of cultural patrimony in the Museum's collection, and shall prepare summaries and notices as required by law.

MODULE 1: THE MERIDIAN MUSEUM AND ITS MISSION

Learning Objectives:
- State the museum's mission.
- Identify the museum's main departments and their roles.
- Describe the museum's history in two or three sentences.

The Meridian Museum is a private, non-profit institution dedicated to preserving and interpreting the history and culture of the Ohio River Valley. We collect, care for, and exhibit objects that tell the story of the people who lived and worked here, from the earliest Native American communities to the present day.

Our mission: "To inspire curiosity about the past and foster a sense of place through collecting, preserving, and interpreting the stories of the Ohio River Valley."

The museum was founded in 1932 by a group of local historians and civic leaders. It has been in its current building since 1968, when the main gallery wing was added. A second expansion, the Riverfront Education Wing, opened in 2015 and houses our classrooms, the Education Office, and the community meeting room.

Departments you should know:

- Director's Office. Oversees all museum operations, fundraising, and community relations.
- Collections. Responsible for the care, documentation, and storage of all objects in the museum's collection. You will learn more about working with Collections in Module 4.
- Curatorial. Researches the collection, plans exhibitions, and writes interpretive text.
- Education. Your primary point of contact for training. Education staff lead tours, school programs, public programs, and volunteer coordination.
- Guest Services. Manages the front desk, admissions, and the museum store.
- Facilities. Maintains the building, grounds, and climate control systems.
- Security. Manages building access, alarms, and the safety of visitors, staff, and the collection.

The museum is governed by a Board of Trustees. The Board meets quarterly. If you are asked to attend a Board meeting to help set up the room, please check with Facilities about the room layout and with Guest Services about the coffee service.

Everyone who works with the museum, whether paid or unpaid, must complete the Meridian Museum Intern Handbook. This is the main reference for all policies and procedures. The handbook is kept in the Education Office and a copy is always available at the front desk. You should also have been given a copy during your first week. If you do not have one, ask your supervisor. The handbook is updated from time to time, so always check that you are using the most recent version. The current edition was revised on 2023-08-15. If you find a copy that is older, please let the Education Curator know so it can be replaced.

The handbook covers topics such as:

- The museum's mission and history.
- Department roles and contacts.
- Safety and emergency procedures.
- Handling and reporting accidents.
- Rules for interacting with visitors.
- Dress code.
- Confidentiality.
- Hours and time tracking.

You do not need to memorize the handbook. You do need to know where to find information in it and to follow it.

3.3 Training for Volunteers

Volunteer training happens in two parts: general orientation and role-specific training.

General orientation is offered once a month, usually on the first Saturday. It lasts about two hours. The orientation covers the museum's mission, basic safety, and a tour of the building. It is led by a staff member from Education, often the Volunteer Coordinator.

Role-specific training is arranged by the department where the volunteer works. For example, a volunteer in Collections will receive training on handling objects. A volunteer in Guest Services will learn how to use the admissions system. This training is usually done one-on-one or in small groups, and it is led by a staff member or an experienced volunteer.

New volunteers should complete general orientation before they start their role-specific training. In most cases, this happens within the first two weeks.

3.4 Training for Interns

Intern training follows a similar pattern but is more structured. Interns must complete the following before their first day of direct work with the public:

- General orientation (same as volunteers).
- A tour of the Collections storage area.
- A review of the Intern Handbook.
- A meeting with their assigned supervisor to set goals.

Interns are also required to attend a weekly check-in meeting. These meetings are held on Fridays at 3:00 PM in the Riverfront Education Wing, Room 204. The check-in is a chance to ask questions, share progress, and get feedback. It is also a chance to meet other interns.

Interns are expected to keep a simple log of their hours and activities. The log is not a diary. It is a record of what you did and how long it took. This log is useful for your supervisor and for your school, if you are receiving credit.

3.5 The Role of the Mentor

Every new intern is assigned a mentor. The mentor is a staff member or a very experienced volunteer who can answer questions and offer guidance. Your mentor is not your supervisor. They are someone you can go to with small questions without feeling like you are bothering your boss.

Mentors are asked to:

- Check in with their assigned intern at least once a week.
- Be available by email or phone.
- Introduce the intern to other staff and volunteers.
- Help the intern understand unwritten rules, like where to park and which break room is quietest.

If you are asked to be a mentor, thank you. It is an important job. If you are an intern and you do not know who your mentor is, ask your supervisor.

You are responsible for tracking your own training hours. A training log form is available at the Volunteer Desk and on the volunteer page of the Museum website. The form asks for the date, the module name, the instructor's name, and the number of hours. Completed forms should be turned in to the Volunteer Coordinator's office (Room 112) by the 5th of the month following the training.

Your training hours are recorded in your volunteer file. You can ask the Volunteer Coordinator to see your file at any time. Please check your record at least once a month. Mistakes are easier to fix if they are caught early.

The Volunteer Handbook specifies that required training hours is 8 hours. This includes the five required modules listed above. If you complete a module more than once (for example, to refresh your skills), the hours count only once toward the 8-hour requirement. The Handbook is available at the Volunteer Desk and in the break room. It is also posted on the volunteer page of the Museum website. If you have not received a copy, ask the Volunteer Coordinator.

The following count toward the 8 required training hours:

- Time spent in the required modules listed in Section 3.6.1.
- Time spent in role-specific training that is required by your position description. This is only if the role-specific training is listed as a requirement for your position. Check with your supervisor if you are unsure.

The following do not count toward the 8 hours:

- General orientation. Orientation is required, but it is not counted as part of the 8 training hours.
- The weekly check-in meeting for interns. This is separate from volunteer training.

3.6.4 Completing Your Training

You must complete all required training within 60 days of your start date. If you do not, you will not be scheduled for any shifts until the training is complete. Extensions may be granted in unusual circumstances, but you must request an extension in writing (email is fine) before the 60-day deadline.

When you have finished all required modules, turn in your completed training log. The Volunteer Coordinator will review the log and mark your file as "training complete." You will receive a confirmation email. Keep this email. You may be asked to show it when you start a new role or when you renew your volunteer badge.

3.6.5 Refresher Training

All volunteers are required to attend a refresher session once every two years. The refresher covers changes to Museum policies and a brief review of safety procedures. It is a single session, 90 minutes long. The refresher does not count toward the 8 required training hours. It is tracked separately in your volunteer file.

## 3.7 Emergency Procedures

All volunteers and interns must be familiar with the emergency procedures in this section. Please read it carefully and ask your supervisor if anything is unclear. Knowing what to do in an emergency can protect you, our visitors, and the collections in your care.

### 3.7.1 General Rules

- Remain calm.
- Follow the instructions of Museum staff and emergency responders.
- Never put yourself at risk to save an object. Objects can be replaced or repaired; people cannot.
- If you are unsure whether something is an emergency, treat it as one and call for help.
- Keep hallways, exits, and stairwells clear at all times. Do not store carts, ladders, or personal items in these areas, even temporarily.
- Know the location of the nearest exit, fire alarm pull station, and fire extinguisher in every area where you work.
- Report any safety hazard you notice (slippery floor, loose railing, obstructed exit, etc.) to the Facilities Office or your supervisor as soon as possible.

### 3.7.2 Medical Emergencies

If someone is injured or becomes ill:

1. Call 911 immediately if the situation is life-threatening or you are unsure of the severity.
2. For non-life-threatening situations, call the Museum's Security Desk at ext. 4111. The Security Officer on duty will dispatch a first aid responder.
3. Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger (e.g., fire, falling debris).
4. Stay with the person until help arrives.
5. Send someone to the main entrance to guide emergency responders to your location, if possible.

First aid kits are located at the Security Desk, the Volunteer Office, and the Education Studio. Automated External Defibrillators (AEDs) are located at the Security Desk, the second floor elevator lobby, and the loading dock.

### 3.7.3 Fire

If you discover a fire or smell smoke:

1. If the fire is small and you have been trained to use a fire extinguisher, you may attempt to put it out. Always keep your back to an exit. If the fire does not go out immediately, leave.
2. If the fire is large, or you are unsure, pull the nearest fire alarm and leave the building.
3. Call 911 from a safe location. Then call the Security Desk at ext. 4111.

When you hear the fire alarm:

- Stop what you are doing.
- Alert visitors near you and direct them to the nearest exit. Use a calm, firm voice.
- Do not use elevators.
- Do not stop to collect personal belongings.
- Close doors behind you as you leave, if it is safe to do so.
- Proceed to the designated assembly area. The assembly area for the main building is the lawn across Meridian Street, in front of the Museum. The assembly area for the Annex is the parking lot across the service drive.
- Report to your supervisor or a Security Officer at the assembly area so they know you are out of the building.

Fire drills are held at least twice a year. When the alarm sounds, treat it as a real emergency. Do not assume it is a drill.

### 3.7.4 Severe Weather

The Museum has a weather radio in the Security Office that is monitored during all open hours. In the event of a tornado warning for Meridian County, the following procedure is used:

1. The Security Desk will announce "Code Weather" over the intercom.
2. Move all visitors and staff to the interior hallways on the first floor and the lower level. Stay away from windows and exterior walls.
3. The restrooms and the stairwells may also be used as shelter areas.
4. Do not use elevators.
5. Remain in the shelter area until the Security Desk announces "All Clear."

## 4. Visitor Experience and Customer Service

### 4.1 Why Visitor Experience Matters

The Meridian Museum is a public trust. Every visitor who walks through our doors—whether a first-time tourist, a school group, a long-time member, or a family with young children—deserves to feel welcome, safe, and respected. Our collections are the reason people come, but the experience they have while they are here is the reason they return, tell their friends, leave a positive review, or become members.

Good customer service is not about being perfect. It is about being present, helpful, and kind. This section covers the basics of engaging with visitors, handling common questions, and managing difficult situations. All staff, volunteers, and interns are expected to read this section and complete the associated quiz in the Learning Management System.

### 4.2 The Meridian Way: Core Principles

These four principles guide every interaction you have with visitors:

1. **Acknowledge.** Make eye contact, smile, and greet visitors when they are within about ten feet of you. A simple "Good morning, welcome to the Meridian" is enough. Do not wait for the visitor to speak first.
2. **Listen.** Let the visitor finish their question or request before you respond. If you are unsure what they are asking, ask a clarifying question like, "Are you looking for the restrooms or the elevator?"
3. **Assist.** Help the visitor to the best of your ability. If you do not know the answer, say so, and then find someone who does. Never guess or make up information about the collection, hours, or events.
4. **Thank.** End the interaction with a genuine thank you, even if you were not able to fully resolve the visitor's issue. "Thank you for letting us know" goes a long way.

### 4.3 Common Visitor Questions and How to Answer Them

Visitors will ask you a wide range of questions. The most common ones are listed below with sample answers. Please familiarize yourself with these so you can respond confidently.

| Question | Suggested Answer |
|----------|------------------|
| "What time do you close?" | "We close at 5:00 PM today. The galleries begin clearing at 4:45, so you have about an hour and a half. Is there a particular gallery you wanted to see?" |
| "Where are the restrooms?" | "There are restrooms on the first floor, just past the coat check, and on the second floor near the American Art gallery. There is also a family restroom on the lower level." |
| "Is there a place to eat?" | "The Meridian Café is on the lower level and is open until 4:30. There are also vending machines near the coat check. You are welcome to bring your own food, but we ask that you eat only in the Café or the picnic tables outside." |
| "Do you have a coat check?" | "Yes, the coat check is free for members and $2 per item for non-members. It is located just inside the main entrance. Large backpacks and umbrellas must be checked." |
| "Can I take photos?" | "Photography for personal use is allowed in most galleries, but flash, tripods, and selfie sticks are not permitted. A few special exhibitions are no-photography; look for the camera-with-a-slash sign at the gallery entrance." |
| "Where is the gift shop?" | "The Museum Store is just off the main lobby, to the right of the entrance. It is open the same hours as the Museum." |
| "Is the Museum accessible?" | "Yes. All public areas are wheelchair accessible. We have wheelchairs and walkers available at the coat check on a first-come, first-served basis. You can also borrow a sensory kit at the front desk." |
| "Do you have a discount for teachers/seniors/military?" | "Yes—we offer reduced admission for seniors, students, and active military. Teachers receive free admission with a valid school ID. You can ask at the Admissions Desk for details." |
