**Module 7: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion in Collections Work**

**Estimated time to complete:** 45 minutes
**Format:** Self-paced reading, followed by discussion questions at your next team meeting

---

**7.1 Why This Module Exists**

The Meridian Museum cares for objects, but we also care for the people who made them, the people
who use them, and the people who have yet to see them. For a long time, museums in this country
told a narrow story. The people who collected, cataloged, and displayed objects often came from
similar backgrounds, and the decisions they made reflected that. The result was that many
communities—and many objects—were left out of the record, or were described in ways that were
inaccurate or even harmful.

This module is not meant to make you feel guilty about the past. It is meant to give you tools for
the present. Every object in our care came from somewhere, and every record we create will be read
by someone. Our job is to make sure that both the objects and the records are treated with respect.

**7.2 Key Terms**

- **Equity:** Giving people what they need to participate fully, which is not the same as giving
  everyone the same thing.
- **Inclusion:** Making sure that people who have been excluded—by race, class, disability,
  language, or any other factor—are actively welcomed and heard.
- **Provenance:** The history of ownership and custody of an object. This is not just a list of
  names and dates; it is a story about power, and we need to read it carefully.
- **Cultural sensitivity:** Understanding that an object may have meanings that are sacred,
  private, or restricted, and that those meanings may not be visible in the catalog record.

**7.3 What This Means for Your Day-to-Day Work**

You may not think of yourself as a "collections" person. You might be a floor guard, a front desk
assistant, or a volunteer in the education department. But everything you do touches the
collection. When you answer a question about an object, you are representing the Museum. When you
write a condition note, you are creating a record that someone else will read. The habits below
apply to everyone.

**When you speak with visitors:**

- Use the language the visitor uses. If they say "the Native American room," you can gently say,
  "The First Peoples gallery." But do not correct them in a way that makes them feel unwelcome.
- If you do not know the answer to a question about an object's history, say so. It is better to
  say "I don't have that information, but I can write your question down for the curatorial team"
  than to guess.
- Be aware that some visitors come to the Museum because an object is connected to their family,
  their nation, or their faith. Treat those visitors with extra care. If they seem upset, offer to
  find a quiet place to talk.

**When you handle objects:**

- The way we describe an object matters. Avoid words that are judgmental or dismissive, like
  "primitive," "exotic," or "quaint." If you see those words in an old catalog record, do not
  repeat them. Make a note for the registrar so the record can be reviewed.
- Some objects are not meant to be seen by everyone. This is especially true for objects related
  to Indigenous ceremonies or to certain religious practices. If you are asked to retrieve an
  object and you are not sure whether it is restricted, ask your supervisor before you do
  anything.
- When you fill out a condition report, stick to the facts. Describe what you see—a scratch, a
  crack, a stain—without interpreting why it is there. You do not know the story. The object may
  have been damaged deliberately, or it may have been damaged in an accident. Your job is to
  record, not to judge.

**Module 7: Documentation and Record-Keeping**

**7.1 Why This Module Matters**

Every object in the Museum has a story, and the written record is how we keep that story
straight. The collection contains more than 40,000 objects, and no single person can remember
the details of all of them. When you write something down, you are not just filling out a form.
You are making sure that the next person—whether they start next week or in twenty years—will
be able to find the same information you have.

This module covers the basics of how we document the collection: what to write, where to write
it, and how to avoid common mistakes. It applies to everyone, not just the registrar's office.
If you work with objects, you will create records. Make them good ones.

**7.2 The Three Kinds of Records**

We keep three main types of records about the collection. They serve different purposes, and
you should know which one you are looking at.

1.  **Catalog records.** These are the official, permanent records of what the Museum owns.
    They live in the collections database (we use a system called TMS, short for The Museum
    System). A catalog record contains the object's unique ID number, a description, the
    name of the person who gave or sold it to us, and its history of locations. Only trained
    staff can edit catalog records. If you see a mistake in one, do not fix it yourself.
    Report it to the registrar.

2.  **Condition reports.** These are records of the physical state of an object at a
    particular moment. We fill them out when an object arrives, when it leaves on loan, when
    it comes back, and whenever we notice a change. Condition reports are attached to the
    catalog record in TMS, but they are also printed and kept in the object's paper file.

3.  **Location records.** These track where an object is right now. The location is the
    room, the storage unit, and the shelf or drawer. Location records are updated every time
    an object moves. If you move an object for any reason, even for a few minutes, you must
    update the location record when you are done. A location that is wrong is almost as bad
    as a missing object.

**7.3 How to Write a Good Condition Report**

You will most often be asked to fill out a condition report. Here are the guidelines.

**Be specific.** Do not write "scratch on base." Write "1.5 cm scratch on the front edge of
the wooden base, running parallel to the grain, from the center toward the right corner."
Use a ruler. Estimate only when you must, and say "approx." when you do.

**Describe, do not diagnose.** You may notice that a ceramic bowl has a crack. You do not
know whether the crack was caused by a drop, by a change in temperature, or by the object's
own age. Write "hairline crack, 4 cm, running from the rim down the side" and leave the
cause out of it. The conservator will figure out the cause.

**Use the clock method for location.** When you need to describe where a mark or damage is
on a flat surface, imagine the object as a clock face. "Stain at 3 o'clock" means the stain
is on the right side of the object as you face it. This is a standard convention, and it
prevents confusion.

**Do not clean the object.** This is important. If you see dust or dirt, do not wipe it off.
Dust can be abrasive, and some materials are water-soluble. Just record what you see. The
conservation department has its own procedures for cleaning.
